1.pericope_label: Four invitations to meet in the plain of Ono, and four times the same refusal

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the parenthesis about the doors for a note of historical accuracy, intimating that what had been said earlier of their setting up was written by way of anticipation, and he observes that the three ringleaders always have the pre-eminence in these lists. On the invitation he notices that Tobiah is dropped from it, appearing only as Sanballat’s secretary, since in the Hebrew of the first verse he is not distinguished from Sanballat by a separate preposition as Geshem is. He names a particular village in the plain of Ono and places that plain on the borders of Philistia, more than twenty miles from Jerusalem. Of the exchange as a whole he counts four attempts under various pretexts with the intention of doing Nehemiah personal harm, each met with the answer that he was finishing his own work, not without a touch of irony — an answer, he adds, of universal application which preachers have known how to use. Keil and Delitzsch read the same parenthesis as a sentence limiting the statement just made, and gloss the opening verb as an impersonal passive, it was heard by him in the indefinite sense of its coming to his ears, noting that such passives grow more frequent in later Hebrew; the rest of the enemies they identify from the earlier chapter as Ashdodites and other hostile individuals. They put Nehemiah’s reason at its most practical, that he could not undertake the journey because his presence in Jerusalem was necessary to the uninterrupted prosecution of the building, and they note that the phrase for answering them in the same manner has a parallel in the second book of Samuel.

Gill reads the report at its strongest, that the wall was quite finished. Of the refusal he marks a detail of manner, that Nehemiah showed them no open contempt and did not even return answer by the messenger who came from them, but sent some of his own people instead. He accounts for the persistence simply, that they were very desirous of getting him into their hands and therefore grew pressing and importunate.

Clarke supposes Ono to have been in the tribe of Benjamin, near Jordan, and says plainly what the invitation was for: they wished to get Nehemiah out of Jerusalem and away from his friends, that they might either carry him off or murder him. On the famous answer he makes the reticence a calculation, that though Nehemiah knew their design he did not think it prudent to mention it, for had he done so they would probably have gone to extremities on finding themselves discovered, and perhaps have attacked Jerusalem while it was ill provided, their preference being to work by treachery rather than open violence; and he finds in the words a form of speech suitable to any man employed on important labours who is invited to remit his work for useless or trivial conferences. Wesley gives the pretext rather than the purpose, that they proposed to consult about the common service of their master the king of Persia, or to make a friendly accommodation, and from the four attempts he draws the rule that we must never be overcome by the greatest importunity to do anything ill or imprudent, but must resist the same temptation with the same reason and resolution — a rule he states almost in Henry’s words.

Henry explains the choice of a village rather than a city, lest the place itself should excite a suspicion that they intended to secure him, and judges that they would have had Nehemiah think they coveted his friendship. He admires what the answer withholds: Nehemiah says nothing of his jealousies and does not reproach them with their treacherous design, but gives them a good reason, and one of the true reasons, for staying where he was, since his care was that the work might not cease, and compliment must always give way to business. He judges the repeated refusal to have been very vexatious to them, because it was the ceasing of the work they aimed at all along, and it must have made them despair of breaking the undertaking to see the undertaker so intent upon it. From the four attempts he draws the rule that we must never suffer ourselves to be overcome by the greatest importunity to do anything sinful or imprudent, but must meet the same temptation with the same reason and resolution, and he applies it to those tempted into idle merry meetings by vain companions, who should answer that they have work to do and must not neglect it.

On the borders of Philistia, more than twenty miles from Jerusalem

He gives a good reason and one of the true reasons, without reproaching them; compliment must give way to business
Simply that his presence was necessary to the uninterrupted prosecution of the building

Alone in noticing that Nehemiah did not reply by his enemies’ own messenger but sent people of his own.

though at that time I had not set up the doors upon the gates
Come, let us meet together in some one of the villages in the plain of Ono. But they thought to do me mischief

5.pericope_label: The open letter charging Nehemiah with making himself king, his denial, and the prayer for strength

schools.summary: Clarke takes the unsealed letter for a studied insult to a man of Nehemiah’s quality, since letters sent to chiefs and governors in the East are always folded into costly silken bags and sealed, so that the detail marks Sanballat’s contempt. He glosses the prophets of the accusation as persons pretending a commission to preach and crying that Nehemiah reigneth, and reads the invitation which follows as an order to come and justify himself, which was a trick to get him into Sanballat’s power. Of the reply he says that Nehemiah would not trouble himself about a charge his accuser knew to be false. Wesley reads the openness of the letter as a claim about its contents, as speaking of a thing commonly known, and renders the letter’s own ostensible sense, that they now had a king of their nation and that the counsel proposed was to examine the matter impartially and clear his innocency; of the prayer he says it is a good one when we are entering on any particular services or conflicts in our Christian warfare.

Ellicott makes the unsealed bag a change of tactics rather than a slight, left open in the hope that Nehemiah would be alarmed by the thought that the people had already read what was in it. He notices that Nehemiah can reproduce the very document, down to its dialectal change of Geshem into Gashmu, and sets out its machinery: Sanballat represents Geshem as circulating a report which, once it reached the distant king, would be read as rebellion, hints that the nations would side with the king, and refers the prophecies of a future King to Nehemiah’s ambition before proposing friendly counsel to avert the danger. He adds that Nehemiah perceived it was not God but Shemaiah himself who had uttered the prophecy against him, and that the man was hired to bring the governor into discredit as a violator of law. Of the prayer he marks the absence of the address to God, which has here been inserted, calling the petition all the more remarkable for the want of it, and counts it among the sudden interjectional prayers that abound in the narrative. Keil and Delitzsch confirm the form of the name from the earlier chapter and press the grammar, the participle being used of what a man intends or prepares to do, so that the charge is that he means to become their king, and the particle carrying the sense that for no other reason than rebellion does he build the wall. They explain the choice of an open letter by the same end, that accusations which anyone might read would oblige Nehemiah to come and clear himself at an interview, and they rule against reading the closing words as a resolution on the ground that the verb is an imperative, the rendering in the first person of the imperfect, I strengthened, which the Septuagint, the Vulgate and the Syriac adopt, being merely an attempt to fit into their context words the translators did not understand.

Gill attends to the sender, that Sanballat now writes in his own name with neither Tobiah nor Geshem joining him, being more solicitous than any of them to get Nehemiah into his hands, and perhaps pretending more friendship than the rest by writing as though they knew nothing of it. He marks the breadth of the report, that it was no whisper among a few but common talk in divers nations and in everybody’s mouth. On the charge of hiring prophets he makes the sharpest observation of any of them, that Sanballat said it to cover what he and Tobiah had themselves been doing, tampering with and corrupting and hiring the prophets to discourage Nehemiah and put him upon methods by which the work would cease.

Henry notes that the best men have lain under the imputation of faction and sedition even in their most innocent performances, and that it is common for what is only the sense of the malicious to be falsely represented as the sense of the many; Sanballat pretends to inform Nehemiah as a friend, that he might hasten to court to clear himself or else stay his proceedings, so that his words were softer than oil while war was in his heart. Nehemiah, he says, denied not only that the things were true but that they were reported, being better known than to be thus suspected. On the closing words he reports that some read them not as a prayer but as a holy resolution, I will now strengthen my hands, precisely because the address to God is supplied by the translators and not in the text; and he adds that Christian fortitude is sharpened by opposition, so that every temptation to draw us from duty should quicken us the more to duty.

debates.question: Why was the fifth letter sent unsealed?

positions.view: As a studied insult, since letters to governors were folded into silken bags and sealed
As intimidation: Nehemiah was to fear that the people had already read it
As a claim that its contents were already commonly known

debates.question: Is "strengthen my hands" a prayer or a resolution?

positions.view: Some read it as a resolution, I will strengthen my hands, since the address to God is supplied and not in the text
A prayer, and the verb is imperative; the versions’ "I strengthened" is an attempt to fit words they did not understand
A prayer, the more remarkable for the absence of the inserted address to God; one of the book’s interjectional petitions

outliers.claim: Alone in reading the accusation as projection, that Sanballat charged Nehemiah with hiring prophets to cover his own hiring of them — which the next paragraph of the chapter proves.
Alone in taking the dialectal spelling Gashmu as evidence that Nehemiah is quoting the actual letter.

themes: Then sent Sanballat his servant unto me in like manner the fifth time with an open letter in his hand
It is reported among the heathen, and Gashmu saith it, that thou and the Jews think to rebel
for which cause thou buildest the wall, that thou mayest be their king
thou hast also appointed prophets to preach of thee at Jerusalem, saying, There is a king in Judah
There are no such things done as thou sayest, but thou feignest them out of thine own heart
Now therefore, O God, strengthen my hands

10.pericope_label: Shemaiah’s hired prophecy, Nehemiah’s refusal to shelter in the temple, and the prayer against the hirelings

schools.summary: Gill offers two places for Shemaiah’s confinement, either his own house or a chamber in the temple, as though he had given himself up to meditation, fasting and prayer, or else, as he might have suggested to Nehemiah, for safety, designing it as an example to him; he may have been a priest of the course of Delaiah, and Nehemiah plainly thought well of him, since he went to his house to consult him on the letters his enemies had sent. Of the refusal he makes Nehemiah the king’s commissioner, who had the conducting and management of the whole affair and on whom it wholly depended, since were he to absent himself the people would depart and leave the wall defenceless, which was the very thing hoped for from the scheme. He perceived that God had not sent the man because the advice was against the cause of God and true religion; and of the closing appeal he reads a request for requital, that God would not only confound and disappoint their wicked counsels but reward them as they deserve.

Wesley puts Shemaiah in a chamber adjoining the temple, on a pretence of singular devotion and communion with God and a further pretence of certain knowledge by the Spirit concerning their approaching danger, from which they could be safe nowhere but in the temple; and he foresees the cost of compliance, that the people would have left their work and every man shifted for his own safety. On the refusal he presses the governor’s obligation, that the life of the whole city and nation in great measure depended on his presence, that he had professed such resolution and courage and confidence in God and had had such eminent experience of God’s assistance, so that flight would dishonour God and religion and betray the people by cowardice. The sin he defines as going into a place forbidden him, and in such a manner as would have been both sinful and shameful, and the reproach as being thought a coward conscious of his own guilt, made contemptible and odious both to his own people and to the king of Persia. Clarke has Shemaiah living in a sequestered, solitary state, pretending to sanctity and to close intercourse with God, and reads the proposal as an instruction to take sanctuary in the temple as the only place of safety. He counts two losses had it been followed: the people would have been left without a leader and come at once to be an easy prey, and Nehemiah, once shut in the temple, would have had his government declared at an end with Sanballat assuming the reins. On the refusal he has Nehemiah ask whether he should betray his trust and leave the flock without a shepherd, resolving instead to stand at his post and be ready to receive his enemies whenever they came. Of Noadiah he would emend the text, observing that the Hebrew alone makes the person a prophetess while all the versions but the Arabic read Noadiah the prophet, and judging the final letter a mistake.

Ellicott thinks Shemaiah probably a priest, found shut up in his house, who likely sent for the governor and represented himself as in danger from the common enemy, predicting an attempt on Nehemiah’s life that night and proposing that they meet within the temple, in the holy place between the Holiest and the outer court, for security. On the refusal he holds two senses together, first the expression of personal dignity and then of fear, who being as I am, a layman, would go into the temple to save his life — rather, he renders it, and live? He makes the mention of Noadiah, a name referred to nowhere else, a mark of how circumstantial the narrative is and indirect evidence of its truth, and calls the closing appeal an official prophetic prayer in which Nehemiah puts God’s own cause into God’s own hands. Keil and Delitzsch say nothing further is known of this prophet beyond his being one of the lying prophets employed by Sanballat and Tobiah, and define the trap as an attempt to seduce Nehemiah into an illegal step and so give occasion for speaking evil of him. On the ambiguous verb of the refusal they decide for the harder sense: it may mean to save his life, or and save his life, but probably Nehemiah used it of not expiating such a transgression of the law with his life, having in mind the command that the stranger who comes nigh shall be put to death. They note that the emphatic negative precedes the divine name, so that the sense is not God but himself who sent the prophecy, that the plural subject of the hiring agrees grammatically with only the latter name though it refers to both men, and that to shut himself within the holy place would have been a grave desecration of the house of God, giving his enemies occasion to cast suspicion on him as a despiser of God’s commands and so to undermine his authority with the people.

Henry reads the whole episode as a change of method, the enemies having failed to fetch Nehemiah into the country and now trying to drive him into the temple for his own safety, so that he be anywhere but at his work; observing him to be a cautious man they endeavoured to gain their point by making him cowardly. The deeper aim he takes to be mockery, that they meant to bring him to do a foolish thing so as to laugh at him and lessen his interest and influence, which is doing the devil’s own work, who tempts men that he may accuse them and draws them into sin that he may glory in their shame; and he laments both the wickedness of men who would betray the cause of God under pretence of communion with God, and the unhappiness of good men to whom no temptation comes with more force than that which wears a colour of religion and is brought by the hand of prophets. Had Nehemiah complied, he says, the people would have left off their work and thrown down their arms, and the enemies might have demolished the wall without opposition. His reasoning he gives as, another might flee, but not I, adding that when we are tempted to sin we should remember who and what we are. Two things he says Nehemiah dreaded in the advice, offending God and shaming himself, since next to the sinfulness of sin we should dread its scandalousness. Of the closing appeal he insists it is no imprecation at all, Nehemiah asking for no particular judgment but referring the cause to him who knows their hearts, whatever injuries are done us being no warrant to avenge ourselves.

In a chamber adjoining the temple, on a pretence of singular devotion and of knowledge by the Spirit

A legal objection: the verb means not to survive the act, the law condemning the stranger who comes nigh

positions.view: It asks requital, that God confound them and reward them as they deserve
No: he asks no particular judgment but refers the cause to God, since we may not avenge ourselves
An official prophetic prayer, putting God’s own cause into God’s own hands

15.pericope_label: The wall finished in fifty-two days, the enemies cast down, and the nobles’ secret league with Tobiah

schools.summary: Clarke sees no difficulty in the fifty-two days, supposing several thousand workmen each labouring as for God, with much of the old wall still entire, the foundations remaining, the materials at hand and no stones to quarry, so that the rubbish was the chief burden; and he measures the feat against antiquity, calling it little beside what Caesar did in Gaul, or Titus, who threw a wall of five thousand paces round Jerusalem in three days besides thirteen towers, or Alexander, who on the account of Quintus Curtius and Arrian walled Alexandria on the Tanais, nearly eight miles in compass, in between twenty and thirty days. He adds that the shortness of the time needs no wonder because God helped them by an especial providence, so observable that their carnal enemies could discover it. Of the correspondence he reads these verses as showing what Nehemiah was really up against, enemies without and false friends within, with a treacherous traffic between the nobles of Judah and the Ammonites; and he ventures the judgment that had almost any other man stood at the head of Jewish affairs, Jerusalem would never have been re-established. He sets the intermarriage in a longer history, the Jews having been fast intermixing with the heathen before Nehemiah came, so that Ezra had such evils to redress chiefly among the common people, whereas here it is the nobles who are interlinked with the heathen, and so far imbued with the spirit of idolatry as to forget God, his service, their brethren and their own souls.

Ellicott works from the calendar, making the twenty-fifth of Elul about our fifteenth of September and the beginning of the work therefore late in July, soon after Nehemiah’s arrival, and concludes that with the wall only partly overthrown, the materials for restoration at hand and the utmost skill shown in organising the bands of workmen the time will not appear too short — so that there is no need to adopt the suggestion of Josephus that the rebuilding occupied two years and four months. On what the enemies perceived he draws a careful distinction, that the work was wrought of God not miraculously but under the divine sanction and help, and he observes that by the phrase Nehemiah at once triumphs over his foes and gives the glory where it was due, his own heroic part in the work being utterly forgotten. Of the marriages he notes that Shechaniah was of the family of Arah which came over with Zerubbabel, that Tobiah had married his daughter and Tobiah’s son a daughter of Meshullam, one of the builders of the wall, and that this family connection led to a conspiracy by oath to thwart the governor; the names of Tobiah and his son being Hebrew, he infers that though naturalised Ammonites they were probably of Hebrew extraction, which makes the facility with which the affinity was contracted easier to understand. Keil and Delitzsch explain the phrase for being cast down in their own eyes, which occurs only here, from the falling of a countenance and the failing of the heart for courage, so that the enemies sank in their own esteem and felt themselves discouraged. They keep to the idiom of the correspondence, that the nobles multiplied their letters, and treat the passage as a supplementary remark; and they argue, against Bertheau, that the men were associates of an oath, bound to Tobiah personally, and not allies in consequence of a sworn treaty, concluding that the affinity by marriage was itself confirmed by an oath. They add that the high priest was also related to Tobiah, and that both Tobiah and his son bear genuine Jewish names.

Henry notes that the wall was begun and finished in fifty-two days and that we have reason to believe they rested on the sabbaths even so; many were employed and there was room for them, and what they did they did cheerfully because they loved the work, while the threats intended to weaken them quickened them to go on the more vigorously, so that out of the eater came forth meat. In the enemies’ dismay he finds envy as much as shame: they were ashamed of their own confidence and crest-fallen at the disappointment, they envied the prosperity of the Jews and grieved to see Jerusalem walled while the kings of Persia had not permitted them to fortify the cities of Samaria, and they despaired of ever doing the mischief they designed, perceiving that the work was wrought of God — even these heathen having sense enough to see a special providence, to believe that God’s work would be perfect, and to conclude that what is of God is to no purpose opposed. Of the nobles he cannot get past the rank of the offenders, that they had so little sense of honour and of their country’s good, writing with all the freedom and familiarity of friends and welcoming letters in return, from which he concludes that great men are not always wise nor always honest. He presses the mischief of marrying with strangers, that for one heathen converted by it ten Jews were perverted, and puts the whole in a sentence: when once they became akin to Tobiah they soon became sworn to him, for a sinful love leads to a sinful league. He adds that they had the impudence to court Nehemiah himself into the friendship by reporting Tobiah’s good deeds before him, and that they betrayed Nehemiah’s own words to him, which furnished Tobiah with matter for letters to put him in fear.

Gill identifies Elul as the sixth month, answering to part of August and part of September, and marks the occasion of the enemies’ hearing as the finishing of the wall. Of the league he notes that they did not merely correspond with Tobiah in a private manner by letters but bound themselves by an oath to him, to be true to his interest and to do as he should advise them.

debates.question: Could the wall really have been finished in fifty-two days?

positions.view: Yes: much of the old wall stood, the materials were at hand, and antiquity offers greater feats in less time
Yes: the calendar fits, the wall was only partly overthrown and the workmen well organised; Josephus’s two years and four months is unnecessary
Yes, and they rested on the sabbaths even so; the enemies’ threats quickened the work

debates.question: In what sense was the work wrought of God?

positions.view: Not miraculously, but under divine sanction and help
By an especial providence, so observable that carnal enemies could discover it
A special providence the heathen themselves could read, concluding that what is of God cannot be opposed

debates.question: What bound the nobles to Tobiah?

positions.view: An oath taken to him personally, not a sworn treaty; the marriage affinity was itself confirmed by an oath
A family connection by two marriages which led to a conspiracy by oath against the governor
A sinful love leading to a sinful league: once akin to him they were soon sworn to him

outliers.claim: Alone in rejecting Josephus’s two years and four months by name, and alone in observing that Nehemiah’s own heroic part is utterly forgotten in the phrase that gives God the glory.

Alone in defending the fifty-two days by comparison with the wall-building of Titus and of Alexander, and alone in judging that under almost any other leader Jerusalem would never have been re-established.
Alone in disputing with Bertheau over whether the men were bound by a personal oath or by a sworn treaty.

when all our enemies heard thereof, and all the heathen that were about us saw these things, they were much cast down in their own eyes
for they perceived that this work was wrought of our God
in those days the nobles of Judah sent many letters unto Tobiah, and the letters of Tobiah came unto them
